stem:
A 46-year-old male patient who was referred from the local clinic for recurrent flank pain. He had a known history of multiple cysts in both kidneys. His parents also had multiple renal cysts. CT imaging of the abdomen is shown in the figure.

Which one of the followings is NOT an indication to treat this disease with tolvaptan (first use) reimbursed by the National Health Insurance in Taiwan?

options.text: CKD stage 3
eGFR decline ≥5.0 ml/min/1.73m2 within one year
eGFR decline ≥2.0 ml/min/1.73m2/year for 5 years
height adjusted Total Kidney Volume (htTKV) Mayo classification 1C-1E

stem: The Association for the Advancement of Medical Instrumentation (AAMI) external icon in conjunction with the International Standards Organization (ISO) has established chemical and microbiological standards for the water used to prepare dialysate, substitution fluid, or to reprocess hemodialyzers for renal replacement therapy. Which one of the following descriptions is NOT CORRECT in the guidelines of safety water-quality standards for hemodialysis from Taiwan Society of Nephrology?

options.text: The dialysis water should be cultured within plate containing medium with tryptone glucose (TGEA) or Reasoners (R2A) at 37°C for 168 hours. The number of colonies should not exceed more than 300 CFU/mL.
The recommendations lowered the acceptable endotoxin concentration to <0.25 EU/ml by Limulus Amebocye Lysate (LAL) in dialysis water at least annually.
The chemical contaminants within the water system should be tested at least annually in combination with the evaluation of the source water.
The chlorine should be monitored the concentration is below 0.1 mg/l.

stem:
A 58-year-old woman was sent to emergent department due to cough, fever and loss of smell since 3 days ago. She is well except with medical history of hypertension under regular angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitor treatment for 5 years. At ER, her vital signs as body temperature 38.1°C, heart rate was 102 beats/min, respiratory rate 18/min, and blood pressure 152/94 mm Hg. The diagnosis of SARS-CoV-2 infection was confirmed by PCR. Laboratory data was collected as follows:
Plasma: Na+ 135, K+ 2.9, Cl- 111, BUN 32, Cr 1.9, CRP 6.3, Albumin 3.2
Urine: Glucose Negative, Protein 2+, RBC 10-20 /HPF, Osmolality 288, Cr 70, Na+ 77, K+ 18, Cl- 96

2. Which one of the following statements concerning the SARS-CoV-2 induced AKI is NOT CORRECT?

options.text: Proteinuria indicates the damage of glomerular podocyte which express high level of ACE2 in kidney.
The ACE2 expression in kidney is abundant which were times higher than those in lung.
Hematuria indicates injury of mesangial cells which express abundant ACE2 in nephron.
ACE2 is highly expressed in the brush border of proximal tubular cells.

stem: What is the reported annual technique failure rate for patients on peritoneal dialysis due to complications such as peritonitis and catheter malfunction?

A 79 y/o male denied systemic disease. He is a business man and just came back from Vietnam 2 days ago. He suffered from dysuria and nausea. UTI was diagnosed and medicine for UTI were given in Vietnam. However, the dysuria persisted. At admission, urinalysis demonstrated PH 7.0, nitrite 1+, occult blood 1+, RBC 3-5/HPF, WBC 0-5/HPF, Crystal: Not found, Urine culture was pending. Urine color was abnormal as the following figure. Kidney echo demonstrated prostate calcification. What is the MOST likely etiology for urine discoloration/ staining?

options.text: UTI with Pseudomonas infection
Phenazopyridine
Chronic bacterial prostatitis
Domitazol

stem: A 52-year-old kidney transplant recipient presents with progressive graft dysfunction and recurrent Escherichia coli urinary tract infections. A renal allograft biopsy demonstrates dense tubulointerstitial infiltrates of large histiocytes with granular eosinophilic cytoplasm. What is the underlying cellular defect responsible for the development of Malakoplakia in this patient?

options.text: Impaired phagolysosomal fusion and defective bacterial degradation in macrophages
Inherited deficiency of NADPH oxidase leading to impaired respiratory burst
Autoimmune antibody-mediated destruction of renal tubular basement membranes
Aberrant monoclonal light chain deposition within lysosomes of proximal tubules

stem: In the pathogenesis of Malakoplakia, which intracellular second messenger abnormality is most specifically associated with defective lysosomal degranulation and microtubule assembly in affected macrophages?

options.text: Elevated intracellular cyclic AMP (cAMP) levels
Reduced intracellular cyclic GMP (cGMP) levels
Overexpression of Inositol Trisphosphate (IP3)
Depletion of intracellular Phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase (PI3K)

stem: Histological evaluation of a renal lesion in a patient with Malakoplakia reveals sheets of large mononuclear phagocytic cells with abundant granular eosinophilic cytoplasm. What is the specific pathological name designated for these characteristic cells?

options.text: Touton giant cells
Armanni-Ebstein cells
von Hansemann cells
Aschoff giant cells

stem: Which pathognomonic intracytoplasmic or extracellular inclusions characterized by targetoid, concentric laminated basophilic rings are diagnostic for Malakoplakia?

options.text: Mallory-Denk bodies
Russell bodies
Councilman bodies
Michaelis-Gutmann bodies

stem: To confirm the diagnosis of Malakoplakia on a renal biopsy specimen, a special histochemical stain is performed to highlight the calcium phosphate deposits within Michaelis-Gutmann bodies. Which stain yields a dark brown to black concentric ring pattern?

options.text: von Kossa stain
Masson trichrome stain
Congo red stain
Jones silver methenamine stain

stem: A histopathologist suspects Malakoplakia in a renal biopsy showing abundant eosinophilic macrophages. Which stain effectively highlights the carbohydrate moiety and bacterial wall glycolipids present inside von Hansemann cells and early Michaelis-Gutmann bodies?

options.text: Sudan Black B stain
Periodic Acid-Schiff (PAS) stain
Acid-Fast Ziehl-Neelsen stain
Mucicarmine stain

stem: Besides calcium phosphate, Michaelis-Gutmann bodies contain significant mineral deposits of ferric iron. Which histochemical stain demonstrates deep blue concentric rings within these bodies?

options.text: Alcian blue stain
Toluidine blue stain
Prussian blue (Perls) stain
Luxol fast blue stain

stem: Electron microscopy (EM) of a renal biopsy specimen confirmed a clinical suspicion of Malakoplakia. Which ultrastructural finding is characteristic of Michaelis-Gutmann body development?

options.text: Subepithelial electron-dense humps along the glomerular basement membrane
Tubuloreticular inclusions within vascular endothelial cells
Parallel organized microtubular structures with fingerprint appearance
Intraphagolysosomal crystalline hydroxyapatite spicules around degraded bacterial membranes

stem: A 45-year-old female renal transplant recipient on Tacrolimus and Mycophenolate Mofetil develops acute graft dysfunction 3 weeks following a treated Escherichia coli urinary tract infection. Graft biopsy reveals intense tubulointerstitial histiocytic infiltration with von Kossa-positive inclusions. What is the most appropriate initial diagnostic interpretation?

options.text: Renal allograft Malakoplakia secondary to persistent intracellular bacterial infection
Acute T-cell mediated rejection (TCMR) Grade IIB
Calcineurin inhibitor (Tacrolimus) arteriopathy
Adenovirus interstitial nephritis

stem: A 60-year-old male with diabetes presents with left flank pain, fever, and a 4-cm solid, enhancing renal cortical mass identified on contrast-enhanced CT. Nephrectomy or core biopsy demonstrates sheets of von Hansemann macrophages with calcified Michaelis-Gutmann bodies. What is the primary clinical differential diagnosis that this benign inflammatory mass mimics radiologically?

options.text: Renal Oncocytoma
Angiomyolipoma
Renal Cell Carcinoma
Medullary Fibroma

stem: In patients with lower urinary tract involvement of Malakoplakia, cystoscopic examination typically reveals which characteristic gross anatomical feature on the bladder mucosa?

options.text: Papillary exophytic exophytic lesions with delicate fibrovascular cores
Deep linear mucosal ulcerations with surrounding cobblestoning
Multiple dark blue to purple submucosal vascular nodules
Soft, slightly raised, yellowish-tan mucosal plaques or nodules

stem: Which class of antimicrobial agents is considered first-line targeted medical therapy for Malakoplakia due to its superior intracellular tissue accumulation within macrophage lysosomes?

options.text: Fluoroquinolones (e.g., Ciprofloxacin)
Third-generation Cephalosporins (e.g., Ceftriaxone)
Aminoglycosides (e.g., Gentamicin)
Carbapenems (e.g., Meropenem)

stem: In addition to Fluoroquinolones, which oral antimicrobial agent exhibits excellent macrophage lysosomal penetration and serves as a primary alternative first-line therapy for renal Malakoplakia?

options.text: Amoxicillin-Clavulanate
Trimethoprim-Sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX)
Nitrofurantoin
Fosfomycin tromethamine

stem: Which pharmacological agent is co-administered in Malakoplakia to increase intracellular cyclic GMP (cGMP) levels and enhance phagolysosomal fusion efficiency in impaired macrophages?

options.text: Atropine
Sildenafil
Bethanechol
Theophylline

stem: A kidney transplant recipient diagnosed with allograft Malakoplakia is started on oral Ciprofloxacin and Bethanechol. Which modification in maintenance immunosuppressive therapy is critical to support clinical resolution of the lesion?

options.text: Immediate pulse administration of High-Dose Methylprednisolone
Addition of Antithymocyte Globulin (ATG) infusion
Switching from Tacrolimus to High-Dose Belatacept
Reduction in the dosage of Calcineurin Inhibitor and/or Antimetabolite agents

stem: A 7-year-old child presents with progressive, painful subcutaneous nodules that rapidly spread to involve deep skeletal muscles and fascia of the lower extremities, leading to severe joint contractures and restricted mobility. Biopsy confirms extensive intramembranous heterotopic ossification involving deep muscular tissue. Serum calcium, phosphate, intact PTH, and TSH are completely normal. Genetic testing reveals a paternal GNAS inactivating mutation. Which of the following rare clinical entities is diagnosed?

options.text: Fibrodysplasia Ossificans Progressiva (FOP)
Pseudohypoparathyroidism Type 1a (PHP-1a)

Familial Tumoral Calcinosis

stem: The displayed sieving curves compare high-flux and medium-cutoff membranes. Which inference best follows from the relative positions of beta-2 microglobulin and albumin?

options.text: Medium-cutoff membranes extend larger middle-molecule removal while limiting, but not eliminating, albumin loss
High-flux membranes remove albumin more completely than beta-2 microglobulin
Medium-cutoff membranes improve only small-solute clearance without changing molecular selectivity
Both membranes have identical retention onset and molecular-weight cutoff

Amiodarone
Allopurinol
Metoprolol

paperTitle: 2026 腎臟專科 Fabry Disease (法布瑞氏症與法布瑞腎病) 主題式練習題庫
stem: Migalastat is an oral pharmacological chaperone approved for Fabry disease. What is its mechanism of action and primary prerequisite for patient selection?

options.text: Irreversibly inhibits lysosomal degradation enzymes; eligible for all patients regardless of gene mutation
Cleaves circulating Gb3 into non-toxic metabolites; restricted to patients with end-stage renal disease
Binds and stabilizes specific amenable mutant forms of Alpha-galactosidase A in the endoplasmic reticulum to promote proper lysosomal trafficking
Suppresses hepatic substrate synthesis by inhibiting glucosylceramide synthase

stem: A 65-year-old male with severe heart failure receives a high-dose continuous intravenous infusion of furosemide. He suddenly complains of tinnitus and bilateral hearing loss. The ototoxicity is primarily mediated by the inhibition of which transporter in the inner ear?

options.text: Na-K-2Cl cotransporter 1 (NKCC1)
Na-Cl cotransporter (NCC)

options.text: It is typically irreversible, bilateral, and affects high frequencies first
It is entirely reversible upon discontinuation of the drug
It primarily causes conductive hearing loss due to middle ear effusion

stem: A patient with maternally inherited diabetes and deafness (MIDD) develops proteinuria and a rising serum creatinine. A kidney biopsy is performed. Which of the following is the most frequently observed histological pattern in the kidneys of patients with MIDD?

options.text: Membranous nephropathy
IgA nephropathy
Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis
Minimal change disease

stem: Which of the following immunopathogenetic mechanisms is primarily responsible for Type II Heparin-Induced Thrombocytopenia (HIT)?

options.text: Formation of IgG autoantibodies against Platelet Factor 4 (PF4)-heparin complexes that cross-link FcγRIIa receptors on platelets.
IgA immune complex deposition on vascular endothelial cells leading to IgA vasculitis.
Direct non-immune osmotic lysis of platelets caused by hyperosmolar heparin preparations.
IgM complement activation causing membrane attack complex insertion into megakaryocytes.

stem: A 62-year-old male on unfractionated heparin (UFH) for deep vein thrombosis (DVT) shows a platelet count drop from 240,000/μL to 90,000/μL on Day 7 of therapy. He is clinically stable without bleeding. What is the most appropriate initial step in management?

options.text: Transfuse 2 units of platelets and continue unfractionated heparin while awaiting anti-PF4 ELISA results.
Discontinue unfractionated heparin immediately and initiate a non-heparin anticoagulant such as Argatroban.
Switch unfractionated heparin to therapeutic-dose Low-Molecular-Weight Heparin (LMWH).
Immediately start oral Warfarin monotherapy and monitor INR daily.

stem: In calculating the 4Ts pretest probability score for suspected Heparin-Induced Thrombocytopenia (HIT), which clinical scenario receives the maximum score of 2 points for the 'Timing' category?

options.text: Platelet count fall occurring after Day 14 of heparin exposure without prior heparin history.
Platelet count fall occurring on Day 2 of heparin exposure in a patient with no heparin exposure in the past year.
Platelet count fall occurring between Day 5 and Day 10 of heparin exposure, or within 24 hours if heparin was administered within the past 100 days.
Platelet count fall occurring immediately post-operatively prior to heparin administration.

stem: Which laboratory assay is considered the gold standard functional test with high specificity (>95%) for confirming Heparin-Induced Thrombocytopenia (HIT)?

options.text: Anti-PF4/Heparin ELISA Immunoassay.
Activated Partial Thromboplastin Time (aPTT).
Prothrombin Time / International Normalized Ratio (PT/INR).
Serotonin Release Assay (SRA).

stem: Why is Warfarin monotherapy strictly contraindicated during the acute phase of Heparin-Induced Thrombocytopenia (HIT) when platelets are severely depressed?

options.text: Warfarin rapidly depletes Protein C prior to prothrombin clearance, predisposing to microvascular thrombosis and venous limb gangrene.
Warfarin directly activates platelet FcγRIIa receptors and worsens thrombocytopenia.
Warfarin neutralizes Argatroban clearance and causes acute liver toxicity.
Warfarin induces severe hyperkalemia by inhibiting adrenal 18-hydroxylase.

stem: A 58-year-old female with End-Stage Renal Disease (ESRD) on maintenance hemodialysis develops suspected Heparin-Induced Thrombocytopenia (HIT). Which non-heparin direct thrombin inhibitor is preferred because its elimination is independent of renal clearance?

options.text: Fondaparinux.
Argatroban.
Enoxaparin.
Dabigatran.

stem: Which of the following statements regarding the laboratory screening assay (Anti-PF4/Heparin ELISA) for HIT is correct?

options.text: It has a 100% specificity for clinical HIT, meaning all positive ELISA tests indicate active HIT thrombosis.
It measures functional serotonin release from washed donor platelets.
It has a very high sensitivity (>99%), so a negative result strongly excludes HIT (high negative predictive value).
It cannot detect IgG class antibodies against PF4-heparin complexes.

stem: A patient with confirmed HIT is being treated with continuous Argatroban infusion. The patient's platelet count recovers to 180,000/μL, and Warfarin is overlapping. How should Argatroban be safely discontinued during Warfarin transition?

options.text: Stop Argatroban immediately as soon as Warfarin is prescribed.
Stop Argatroban when the combined INR reaches 2.0.
Administer Vitamin K1 to reverse Argatroban before stopping.
Continue Argatroban co-administration for at least 5 days until the combined INR is >4.0, then stop Argatroban and recheck INR in 4-6 hours.

stem: Why are platelet transfusions generally contraindicated in patients with acute Heparin-Induced Thrombocytopenia (HIT) unless life-threatening hemorrhage occurs?

options.text: Infused platelets provide additional substrate for anti-PF4/heparin antibodies, triggering further activation and thrombotic events.
Transfused platelets rapidly clear Argatroban from the bloodstream.
Transfused platelets cause acute intravascular hemolysis via complement activation.
Transfused platelets induce severe metabolic alkalosis via citrate load.

stem: A 65-year-old male undergoing urgent Percutaneous Coronary Intervention (PCI) has a documented history of acute HIT 2 weeks ago with persistent SRA positivity. Which short-acting intravenous direct thrombin inhibitor is preferred for anticoagulation during PCI?

options.text: Low-Molecular-Weight Heparin.
Bivalirudin.
Warfarin.
Rivaroxaban.

stem: Fondaparinux is a synthetic pentasaccharide used off-label for HIT. What is the major pharmacokinetic limitation of Fondaparinux in patients with severe renal impairment (CrCl <30 mL/min)?

options.text: It undergoes rapid hepatic metabolism via CYP3A4, causing drug interactions.
It directly cross-links FcγRIIa receptors in 100% of patients with HIT.
It is eliminated primarily by the kidneys and accumulates, increasing bleeding risk in renal failure.
It cannot inhibit Factor Xa in the presence of low antithrombin levels.

stem: In a patient undergoing maintenance hemodialysis who develops acute HIT, what is the recommended circuit anticoagulation strategy to maintain dialyzer patency without heparin?

options.text: Low-dose Unfractionated Heparin flushes into the arterial line.
Heparin-coated hemodialysis membranes.
High-dose Low-Molecular-Weight Heparin in the venous bloodline.
Regional Citrate Anticoagulation (RCA) or saline flushes.

stem: What distinguishes Type 1 HIT from Type 2 HIT regarding pathophysiology and clinical course?

options.text: Type 1 HIT is a transient, non-immune direct heparin effect with mild platelet drop and no thrombosis risk, whereas Type 2 HIT is immune-mediated with high thrombosis risk.
Type 1 HIT is IgG-mediated, whereas Type 2 HIT is IgE-mediated anaphylaxis.
Type 1 HIT requires mandatory Argatroban therapy, whereas Type 2 HIT requires no treatment.
Type 1 HIT occurs exclusively with LMWH, whereas Type 2 HIT occurs exclusively with Fondaparinux.

stem: A patient receives Unfractionated Heparin during cardiac surgery 60 days ago. Today, he is re-exposed to UFH for DVT prophylaxis and develops abrupt severe thrombocytopenia within 12 hours. What explains this rapid-onset HIT presentation?

options.text: Direct osmotic damage to platelets by hypertonic heparin solutions.
Circulating anti-PF4/heparin IgG antibodies persisted from the prior heparin exposure within the past 100 days.
Anaphylactoid IgE release from mast cells causing instant platelet destruction.
Acute bone marrow aplasia induced by synthetic heparin preservatives.

stem: What is the main monitoring parameter and target range for guiding continuous intravenous Argatroban infusion in acute HIT management?

options.text: Prothrombin Time (PT), targeted to 4.0 to 5.0 times baseline.
Bleeding Time, targeted to >15 minutes.
Activated Partial Thromboplastin Time (aPTT), targeted to 1.5 to 3.0 times the baseline value.
Serum Creatinine clearance, targeted to >60 mL/min.

stem: A patient with acute HIT develops necrotic skin lesions at heparin subcutaneous injection sites and dark discoloration of the toes. What pathophysiological event has occurred?

options.text: Direct cytotoxic necrosis caused by bacterial contamination of heparin vials.
Type I IgE-mediated immediate hypersensitivity reaction.
Acute cholesterol atheroembolization secondary to heparin-induced plaque rupture.
Widespread microvascular thrombosis driven by intense thrombin generation and platelet microparticle release.

stem: Which of the following is a recognized trigger for HIT in End-Stage Renal Disease (ESRD) patients who are not receiving therapeutic intravenous heparin?

options.text: Routine heparin flushes for central venous hemodialysis catheter lock and maintenance.
Oral Calcium Carbonate phosphate binder therapy.
Subcutaneous Erythropoietin-Stimulating Agent (ESA) injections.
Dialysate bicarbonate concentration of 35 mEq/L.

stem: In a critically ill patient in the ICU with acute HIT and severe acute hepatic failure (Child-Pugh Class C), how should the initial continuous Argatroban infusion rate be adjusted?

options.text: Increase the initial infusion rate to 5.0 μg/kg/min to compensate for liver failure.
Reduce the initial infusion rate significantly (e.g., from 2.0 μg/kg/min down to 0.5 μg/kg/min) and monitor aPTT closely.
Maintain standard dose because Argatroban is cleared by renal hemodialysis.
Switch immediately to therapeutic Warfarin monotherapy.

stem: What is the definition of Autoimmune HIT (or Delayed-Onset HIT)?

options.text: HIT triggered exclusively by natural food products containing endogenous heparin sulfates.
HIT caused by autoantibodies targeting Antithrombin III directly.
HIT characterized by heparin-independent platelet-activating antibodies that persist or begin days after heparin discontinuation.
HIT that resolves spontaneously within 2 hours of heparin administration.

stem: Which of the following physical examination findings is classic for Albright Hereditary Osteodystrophy (AHO) seen in patients with PHP-1a and PPHP?

options.text: Shortening of the 4th and 5th metacarpal bones (Brachydactyly IV/V) and round facies
Elongated digits (Arachnodactyly) and pectus excavatum
Lisch nodules in the iris and cafe-au-lait macules
Bilateral sensorineural hearing loss and ocular coloboma

stem: A 28-year-old male with long-standing untreated PHP-1a presents with extrapyramidal movement symptoms and cognitive decline. Brain CT reveals extensive symmetrical calcification of the basal ganglia. What is the primary pathophysiological driver of intracranial calcification in chronic unmanaged PHP-1a?

options.text: Direct Gsα toxicity on cerebrovascular endothelial cells
Deposition of mutated Gsα protein aggregates in the caudate nucleus
Severe hypomagnesemia leading to brain parenchymal necrosis
Elevated Calcium-Phosphate Product (Ca x Pi) secondary to hyperphosphatemia and high PTH

Allosteric activation of peroxisomal alanine-glyoxylate aminotransferase (AGXT)

By dividing the aldosterone concentration in the adrenal vein by the cortisol concentration in the adrenal vein.
By subtracting the peripheral aldosterone concentration from the adrenal vein aldosterone concentration.
By dividing the aldosterone concentration in the right adrenal vein by the aldosterone concentration in the left adrenal vein.

stem: A kidney allograft biopsy is evaluated for chronic active antibody-mediated rejection. According to the Banff criteria, what degree of peritubular capillary basement membrane multilayering is required to qualify as chronicity, and what finding can substitute for the presence of donor-specific antibodies?

options.text: Severe multilayering with 3 or more layers in at least 2 peritubular capillaries; positive crossmatch substitutes for donor-specific antibodies.
Severe multilayering with 5 or more layers in at least 1 peritubular capillary; diffuse C3 staining substitutes for donor-specific antibodies.
Severe multilayering with 7 or more layers in 1 peritubular capillary or 5 or more layers in 2 peritubular capillaries; linear C4d staining substitutes for donor-specific antibodies.
Mild multilayering with 2 or more layers in 5 peritubular capillaries; intense IgG staining substitutes for donor-specific antibodies.

stem: A 45-year-old patient presents with acute kidney injury, thrombocytopenia, and microangiopathic hemolytic anemia. Renal biopsy confirms thrombotic microangiopathy (TMA). During this acute endothelial injury, which of the following changes in glomerular endothelial cell (GEnC) marker expression is typically observed?

options.text: Downregulation of Tissue Factor and upregulation of Thrombomodulin
Complete loss of CD31 expression with de novo synthesis of Nephrin
Increased expression of von Willebrand factor (vWF) and ICAM-2
Upregulation of PV-1 and loss of integrin alpha-v beta-3

stem: In the evaluation of early diabetic nephropathy, a temporal relationship exists between structural podocyte damage and the development of abnormal proteinuria. When comparing the appearance of urinary biomarkers, which of the following statements most accurately describes the timeline of biomarker sensitivity?

options.text: Microalbuminuria (AER 30-300 mg/day) uniformly precedes any detectable shedding of podocyte-specific proteins.
Urinary nephrin levels peak only after macroalbuminuria (>300 mg/day) has been established for several months.
An isolated elevation in urinary albumin creatinine ratio (UACR) occurs independently of early podocyte architectural changes.
Significant urinary shedding of podocalyxin can be detected prior to the transition from normoalbuminuria to an albumin excretion rate of 30-300 mg/day.

stem: A 70-year-old male with confirmed AL amyloidosis develops progressive dyspnea and lower extremity edema. Echocardiography reveals a thickened left ventricular myocardium. Which of the following combinations of clinical and diagnostic findings is most highly characteristic of cardiac amyloidosis?

options.text: Dilated cardiomyopathy, low NT-proBNP levels, and high-voltage QRS complexes on ECG
Restrictive cardiomyopathy, significant NT-proBNP elevation, and low-voltage QRS complexes on ECG
Hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy, decreased troponin levels, and normal QRS voltage on ECG
Constrictive pericarditis, normal NT-proBNP levels, and prolonged PR intervals on ECG

stem: A 65-year-old female undergoing prolonged neuro-intensive care sedation with high-dose propofol infusion presents with distinct green urine discoloration. Urine laboratory analysis excludes urinary tract infection, hematuria, and bilirubinuria. Which of the following metabolic processes best explains the underlying etiology of propofol-induced green urine?

options.text: Accumulation of phenolic metabolites excreted by the kidneys when hepatic glucuronidation capacity is exceeded.
Direct nephrotoxic destruction of proximal tubular epithelial cells causing excretion of cellular lipofuscin.
Precipitation of insoluble propofol-calcium phosphate microcrystals within the renal collecting ducts.
Induction of hepatic heme oxygenase resulting in massive urinary clearance of biliverdin.

stem: A 6-year-old girl diagnosed with Primary Hyperoxaluria Type I (PH1) is evaluated for disease-targeted therapy. Which novel therapeutic agent works via RNA interference (RNAi) to target glycolate oxidase (HAO1 mRNA) in hepatocytes, reducing hepatic oxalate production?

options.text: Pyridoxine (Vitamin B6) alone
Potassium citrate
Cysteamine
Lumasiran

stem: A nephrologist is evaluating a patient with end-stage renal disease who presents with acute respiratory distress and hemoptysis. Radiographic imaging reveals bilateral airspace opacities. Which of the following statements best describes the pathophysiology and clinical significance of uremic pneumonitis in this context?

options.text: It is primarily caused by an underlying infectious process and requires immediate empirical antimicrobial coverage.
It is characterized by increased alveolar-capillary membrane permeability due to uremic toxins and can clinically mimic an autoimmune pulmonary-renal syndrome.
It is driven by circulating autoantibodies against the alveolar basement membrane, necessitating long-term cyclophosphamide therapy.
It predominantly manifests as unilateral localized consolidation on chest imaging resulting from spontaneous pulmonary infarction.

stem: A 38-year-old male with end-stage kidney disease secondary to focal segmental glomerulosclerosis has been maintained on peritoneal dialysis. He presents with a 1-day history of orthopnea, chest tightness, non-productive cough, and a rapid body weight gain following a recent adjustment to his dialysate regimen for ultrafiltration failure. Physical examination reveals decreased breath sounds over the right lung field but no signs of peritonitis. Chest X-ray demonstrates a massive right-sided pleural effusion. A diagnostic right thoracentesis yields transudative fluid with an elevated pleural-to-serum glucose gradient of 36 mg/dL. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Bacterial pneumonia complicated by parapneumonic effusion
Acute heart failure exacerbation with bilateral pleural effusions
Pleuroperitoneal communication presenting as a right hydrothorax
Malignant pleural effusion related to undiagnosed malignancy

stem: A 31-year-old male with end-stage renal disease is diagnosed with peritoneal dialysis-associated eosinophilic peritonitis shortly after catheter insertion. His dialysate is extremely turbid, yet he denies any abdominal pain or systemic symptoms. When distinguishing this condition from acute bacterial peritonitis and determining the appropriate management plan, which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: sinophilic peritonitis presents with severe abdominal pain and mandates immediate administration of prolonged intraperitoneal antibiotics.
e condition is primarily infectious and requires prompt surgical removal of the peritoneal dialysis catheter.
e routine initial treatment involves switching immediately to continuous venovenous hemofiltration due to the high risk of systemic anaphylaxis.

cognizing the minimal abdominal pain is crucial to differentiate it from bacterial peritonitis, and management may involve low-dose oral glucocorticoids or antihistamines to prevent catheter obstruction.

stem: A 45-year-old male presents with a gradual rise in serum creatinine from a baseline of 1.2 mg/dL to 2.1 mg/dL at 8 months after receiving a deceased-donor kidney transplant. He has been compliant with his immunosuppressive regimen consisting of tacrolimus, mycophenolate mofetil, and prednisone. A kidney allograft biopsy is performed. Based on the timing post-transplant, which of the following is the most likely predominant histopathological finding?

options.text: T-cell mediated rejection
Antibody-mediated rejection
Calcineurin inhibitor toxicity
Recurrent glomerulonephritis

stem: A 57-year-old male is declared brain dead following a massive myocardial infarction. He had no known medical history prior to admission. His terminal serum creatinine is 1.8 mg/dL. In addition to his age and renal function, which of the following criteria must be present for him to be classified as an expanded criteria donor (ECD)?

options.text: A diagnosis of diabetes mellitus for more than 5 years
A documented history of hypertension
A terminal urine output of less than 500 mL in 24 hours
A cold ischemia time exceeding 24 hours

stem: During the procurement of organs from a donor after circulatory death (DCD), physiological parameters are closely monitored to determine the onset of functional warm ischemia time (fWIT). According to standard criteria, which of the following hemodynamic or respiratory thresholds marks the beginning of fWIT?

options.text: Systolic blood pressure drops below 90 mmHg or oxygen saturation falls below 90%
Mean arterial pressure drops below 60 mmHg or respiratory rate falls below 8 breaths per minute
Systolic blood pressure drops below 50 mmHg or oxygen saturation falls below 75%
Heart rate drops below 40 beats per minute or end-tidal CO2 falls below 15 mmHg

stem: An organ procurement organization is managing a donor after circulatory death. Extubation has been performed, and the team is waiting for circulatory arrest. Organ-specific tolerances to functional warm ischemia time (fWIT) must be strictly observed. Which of the following correctly pairs the solid organ with its maximum tolerated fWIT limit?

options.text: Liver: 60 minutes
Pancreas: 120 minutes
Lungs: 30 minutes
Kidneys: 120 minutes

stem: A 61-year-old man with hypercalcemia (serum calcium 12.2 mg/dL), hypophosphatemia (serum phosphorus 2.1 mg/dL), and markedly elevated intact PTH (210 pg/mL) undergoes localization studies for primary hyperparathyroidism. Neck ultrasonography fails to identify any enlarged parathyroid gland. Technetium-99m (99mTc) Sestamibi SPECT/CT demonstrates a focal area of increased radiotracer uptake in the anterior mediastinum, which overlaps anatomically with multiple calcified mediastinal lymph nodes secondary to previous pulmonary tuberculosis. Which of the following statements regarding this scenario is correct?
options: A. Coexisting tuberculous mediastinal lymphadenopathy and calcified nodes can obscure or create diagnostic interference during Sestamibi localization of an ectopic parathyroid adenoma
B. Embryologically, ectopic parathyroid glands originate exclusively from the first pharyngeal pouch and migrate superiorly into the thyroid parenchyma
C. The presence of mediastinal lymphadenopathy rules out primary hyperparathyroidism and confirms isolated extra-renal 1α-hydroxylase production
D. 99mTc-Sestamibi scan uptake is entirely specific for tuberculous granulomas and cannot be retained by parathyroid tissue

stem: To evaluate a peritoneal dialysis patient presenting with unexplained ultrafiltration failure, a modified Peritoneal Equilibration Test (PET) using a 4.25% dextrose solution is conducted. Serial dialysate sodium concentrations are measured. The patient displays a significantly reduced 60-minute sodium dip (sieve reduction in dialysate sodium < 5 mmol/L). Which transport pathway and molecular channel defect is specifically indicated by this blunted sodium dip?
options: A. Diffusional small-pore transport mediated by Endothelial Junctional Claudins
B. Convective large-pore clearance mediated by Intercellular Gaps
C. Active transcellular sodium reabsorption mediated by Epithelial Sodium Channels (ENaC)
D. Ultra-small pore free-water transport mediated by Aquaporin-1 (AQP1)

stem: Which of the following statements regarding the intrarenal hemodynamic effects and clinical monitoring of Sacubitril/Valsartan (ARNI) therapy is correct?
options: A. Neprilysin inhibition leads to increased breakdown of Angiotensin II, which directly dilates the afferent arteriole and increases filtration fraction.

B. Combined Neprilysin inhibition and Angiotensin receptor blockade reduce intraglomerular capillary hydraulic pressure by simultaneously dilating afferent arterioles (via natriuretic peptides) and efferent arterioles (via AT1 receptor blockade).
C. An increase in serum creatinine of greater than 5% within 4 weeks of starting Sacubitril/Valsartan represents irreversible acute tubular necrosis and mandates immediate drug withdrawal.

D. Sacubitril/Valsartan impairs renal autoregulation by selectively constricting both afferent and efferent arterioles, resulting in a dramatic increase in intraglomerular pressure and heavy proteinuria.
